full_article:
KATHMANDU: The United Sherpa Association of Colorado (USAC) has provided $30,406 to the Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund to support victims of the devastating floods that swept through the Bhotekoshi–Trishuli corridors on August 26, killing thousands of people.

Under the leadership of USAC President and social worker Lhakpa Sherpa, executive committee members and community members residing in the United States donated to the fund through USAC.

According to the association, its Nepal Flood Relief Campaign received overwhelming support from the community. “Together, through the kindness and generosity of so many wonderful people, we raised $30,406 for Nepal’s Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund,” said President Lhakpa Sherpa.

On September 14, 2026, USAC wired the full $30,406 raised through the campaign to the Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund. The association separately covered the $40 international transfer fee, ensuring that none of the donated funds went toward that cost, according to Lhakpa.

For transparency, USAC said it is sharing the campaign record, donor list, and transfer receipt. “To everyone who donated, shared our campaign, encouraged others, or helped in any way, thank you from the bottom of our hearts. Your kindness, compassion, and generosity made this possible. This campaign is now officially closed, but our care and connection with those affected continue. We will share updates as we receive information about the ongoing recovery efforts in Nepal,” the association added.

Deadly floods in Nepal, punishing heat waves across the United States and Europe, and wildfire-conducive drought in the American West all show that extreme weather is becoming harder to ignore, according to Inside Climate News.

But even with mounting scientific evidence that a hotter planet is intensifying these events, many people still do not see climate change as part of the story.

Here's what to know

Research summarized by Inside Climate News highlights that extreme weather is happening more often and hitting harder. But public recognition of its connection to climate change has not kept pace.

Anthony Leiserowitz, director of the Yale Program on Climate Change Communication, said many people do not arrive at that link on their own.

"Most people do not automatically, intuitively, on their own, connect that event — a flood, a heat wave, a wildfire — to climate change," Leiserowitz said. "Climate change is still a relatively abstract idea for many, many people."

Research has found an uneven relationship between lived experience and climate views. A 2019 review of 73 papers found mixed results on whether extreme weather changes public opinion on climate change.

A 2024 study found that among climate-fueled weather events, only fires produced a modest but meaningful increase in recognition of global warming and support for action, and even that boost faded quickly.

Leiserowitz said a key obstacle is "psychological distance," meaning how near or personal a crisis feels. When people do not view an event as touching them, their relatives, or their community, they are less likely to treat it as urgent.

More background

That disconnect could also weaken people's ability to prepare for and adapt to climate risks.

Leiserowitz said responses can range widely, and they do not all require the same level of awareness or motivation, whether someone is making smaller household changes or pressing elected officials for larger climate measures.

He also said extreme weather can become a "teachable moment."

"Suddenly, the public, the media and political leaders all focus their very scattered and limited attention on the same event. A lot of this is just about helping people connect the dots for the very first time. And once you've done that, you've taught them something, and they are now primed to make that connection themselves in the future," Leiserowitz said.

The University of Colorado Boulder's Media and Climate Change Observatory found that worldwide climate news coverage has fallen 38 percent from its 2021 high.

Another report from 2025, based on surveys in eight countries, found widespread agreement that climate coverage matters, but only about four in 10 people said the media does a good job explaining the causes of climate change and possible solutions.

Max Boykoff, a professor of environmental studies at the University of Colorado Boulder, told the university, "People typically do not start their day with a cup of coffee and the latest peer-reviewed journal article. Instead, they turn to media — television, newspapers, radio, social media — to understand how science and policies could impact their everyday lives. When the media fail to cover these pressing climate issues abundantly and accurately, people may not recognize how climate change shapes their daily lives, livelihoods and challenges."

What can be done?

Climate attribution science has advanced rapidly. Leiserowitz said that understanding can influence choices at many levels, from putting together an emergency go kit to urging public officials to take stronger climate action.

"If you don't know about climate change, you can't make decisions knowing that the events that you're already experiencing are going to become more frequent, more severe, and there's going to be more surprises," Leiserowitz said. "Now, if you understand that, you can start to take actions to both mitigate the risk to reduce and limit climate change, but you can also be taking the incredibly important actions now that are about preparing for and adapting to that future world."

Where can I learn more?

These stories make that disconnect easier to see. They show deadly heat, rising economic losses, and ecosystem damage playing out in specific places, bringing a global trend down to the local level.

• In global rankings, one country is bearing the brunt as extreme weather losses mount.

• Across the central United States, deadly temperatures envelop communities as millions remain under heat alerts.

• Across Western U.S. cities, history-making heat wave signals the punishing extremes scientists expect more often.

• In the United States, close to the limits of survivability, heat and humidity compound danger.

• In Ecuador and Colombia, disturbing consequences of recent extreme weather are threatening fragile páramo ecosystems.

title: Nepal flood survivors return to ruins as search for missing relatives continues - Türkiye Today
description: Nepal flood survivors return to ruins as search for missing relatives continues  Türkiye Today
publisher.title: Türkiye Today
full_article:
N early three weeks after devastating floods swept through parts of Nepal, survivors in Nuwakot continue to return to what remains of their homes, searching through debris for belongings, while families of missing people keep up their search in hospitals in Kathmandu.

The disaster struck on Aug. 26 after a glacier on Nepal's Mount Langtang Lirung fractured at an altitude of about 5,200 meters (17,060 feet), setting off an ice-rock avalanche that developed into a massive debris flow.

Floodwaters and mudslides devastated the districts of Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, and Kavre, as well as the Kathmandu Valley. The disaster also buried the Gyirong border crossing in Xizang.

Aftermath of devastating flash floods that struck Nepal on August 26 is seen in Nuwakot, where people in the affected areas continue to return to the ruins of their homes, searching for belongings and the last remnants of lives that were swept away, in Bagmati province, central Nepal, on September 14, 2026. (AA Photo)

Survivors return to what is left of their homes

By Sept. 14, people in affected areas of Nuwakot, northwest of Kathmandu, were still going back to the ruins of their homes in hopes of recovering possessions and other remnants of lives swept away by the disaster.

Some survivors searched through piles of debris for anything they could salvage, while others stood where their homes had once been.

Religious figures also visited affected communities to hold prayers for those who died. Some ceremonies continued for one or two days as bereaved families came together to remember their relatives and pray for the peace of their souls.

Aftermath of devastating flash floods that struck Nepal on August 26 is seen in Nuwakot, where people in the affected areas continue to return to the ruins of their homes, searching for belongings and the last remnants of lives that were swept away, in Bagmati province, central Nepal, on September 14, 2026. (AA Photo)

More to Read Nepal flood death toll rises to 1,357 as rescuers search tunnels World 1 min read Nepal rescuers save 4 survivors as flood search enters 12th day World 1 min read

Families search hospitals for missing relatives

The search for people who remain missing has also carried on in Kathmandu, where families have been visiting hospitals and checking photographs and lists displayed on hospital walls.

Some relatives used mobile phone video calls to show the photographs to family members elsewhere, hoping someone might recognize a missing person and help with identification.

Nearly three weeks after the glacier fracture set the disaster in motion, communities across the affected areas continue to deal with destroyed homes, missing relatives and the aftermath left behind by the floods and mudslides.

full_article:
The Landslide Blog is written by Dave Petley, who is widely recognized as a world leader in the study and management of landslides.

In the last few days, two really interesting and useful updates have been published covering the 3-4 October 2023 GLOF in the Teesta Valley in India and the 26 August 2026 landslide in Nepal and Tibet.

Regarding the 3-4 October GLOF in the Teesta Valley in India, the ever-impressive Praful Rao has posted an article on the Save The Hills blog that uses satellite imagery to chronicle the impact of the flood. As Praful puts it:

“…these images provide an important historical record of the largest GLOF in the Himalayas. When juxtaposed with earlier images of the same areas from 2022, they reveal the extraordinary scale and humongous power of nature as the GLOF swept down the Teesta Valley.”

To give you an idea of the scale of this piece of work, here is one of the image pairs that Praful has posted:-

Before and after image of the 2023 Teesta Valley GLOF, posted to the Save The Hills blog by Praful Rao.

And here is a photo, also posted by Praful, of the aftermath of the GLOF in that town, Chungthang:-

The aftermath of the 2023 Teesta Valley GLOF in Chungthang, posted to the Save The Hills blog by Praful Rao.

Turning now to the 26 August 2026 landslide in Nepal and Tibet, the Youth Innovation Lab in Nepal has posted a very interesting review of the event – the document is here as a PDF.

This reports on a workshop convened a couple of weeks after the event by the Youth Innovation Lab with the Red Cross Red Crescent Climate Centre, Kathmandu University and the University of Twente, with the Ministry of Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation. It included local and international experts and it examines the event itself, the response and early lessons learnt.

For example, it provides an initial analysis of the range of parameters involved in the landslide, debris flow and debris flood provided by different analyses:-

The range of parameters involved in the 26 August 2026 landslide, debris flow and debris flood in Nepal and Tibet, from the Youth Innovation Lab report.

There is a huge range of information in this report, including an examination of the potential role of the rapidly changing climate in these high elevation Himalayan regions. It is well worth a read.

The Korea Disaster Relief Team is briefed by local Red Cross officials about last month's devastating floods that hit Rasuwa District near the Nepal-Tibet border, Monday (local time). Courtesy of Korea Disaster Relief Team

A Korean relief team dispatched to Nepal was set to deploy drones Tuesday as part of their search efforts for nine Koreans who remain missing following last month's devastating floods, Seoul's foreign ministry said.

The second contingent of the Korea Disaster Relief Team (KDRT), who arrived in Kathmandu on Friday, was seeking to employ drones for the rescue operation in coordination with Nepali authorities, according to the ministry.

The nine Koreans — six employees of Doosan Enerbility and three of Korea South-East Power — went missing on Aug. 26 after massive floods and landslides hit Rasuwa District near the Nepal-Tibet border while they were working at a hydropower plant construction site.

The eight-member contingent was briefed on the ongoing search missions led by Korean companies and has conducted on-site inspections for reconstruction and recovery efforts in flood-stricken Nepal.

On Saturday, the first 44-member KDRT contingent returned home after a 10-day search-and-rescue mission. The team rescued one Chinese survivor but failed to locate the Koreans still unaccounted for.

More than 1,400 people have been killed, with over 5,600 still missing in Nepal and China's Tibet Autonomous Region following the disaster, according to foreign media reports.

Our Bureau

Montgomeryville, PA

Bharatiya Temple, a prominent Hindu-Jain temple serving the Greater Philadelphia region, will present a $100,000 donation to Sewa International in support of relief and rehabilitation efforts for communities affected by the recent disaster in Nepal.

The ceremonial check presentation will take place on Saturday, September 19, 2026, at 4:00 PM during the Philadelphia Ganesh Festival at Bharatiya Temple.

The funds were raised following a multi-faith prayer gathering held on September 3, 2026, where Hindu, Muslim, Jewish, Sikh, and Christian faith and community leaders came together in prayer, solidarity, and support for the people of Nepal. The gathering raised approximately $100,000 for Nepal relief and rehabilitation efforts.

The collected funds will be presented to Sewa International, a humanitarian nonprofit organization, to support its relief and rehabilitation efforts in Nepal.

The check presentation will take place during the Philadelphia Ganesh Festival, organized by Bharatiya Temple in collaboration with Indian community organizations from throughout the Greater Philadelphia region. The festival brings together thousands of community members to celebrate Indian religious traditions, culture, music, dance, and community service.

This year’s Philadelphia Ganesh Festival is being celebrated from September 14 through September 25, 2026, marking the festival’s 22nd year. September 19 will also feature Outdoor IndiaFest, bringing together religious, cultural, civic, and community leaders for a day of celebration and fellowship.

The Greater Philadelphia Hindu community has a longstanding tradition of supporting humanitarian and disaster-relief efforts both in the United States and around the world. Over the years, the community has mobilized support for numerous humanitarian causes, including assistance related to the Kargil conflict, September 11 attacks, Indian Ocean tsunami, Gujarat earthquake, Hurricane Katrina, Nepal earthquake, and the COVID-19 pandemic.

September 19 Festival Highlights

In addition to the Nepal relief check presentation, the program will include a full day of religious and cultural programming at Bharatiya Temple.

Highlights include:

– Shri Ganesh Maha Abhishekam

– Children’s Ganesh Puja

– Daily Rajopchar Aarti of Lord Ganesha

– Ganrang Dance Competition

– Rajasthani folk music by visiting artists from Rajasthan

– Bharatanatyam recital by Guru Shweta Prachande

– Evening Bollywood orchestra by Kalamanch as a tribute to legendary singer Asha Bhosle

The festival program also includes a special Shehnai presentation by Pandit Lokesh Anand for Lord Ganesha.

title: Price war and flood cloud Nepal EV market - Nepali Times
description: Price war and flood cloud Nepal EV market  Nepali Times
publisher.title: Nepali Times
full_article:
The Rasuwagadi checkpoint that was damaged in last year’s flood had just resumed being the main entry point for EV imports from China when it was hit by the massive debris flow on 26 August.

There is no count of the cars and vans that got washed off the road from the border down the Pasang Lhamu Highway that day.

Before the disaster struck, Kathmandu saw two back-to-back auto shows, the NAIMA and NADA fairs. They showcased an unprecedented number of electric vehicles across the two-, three-, four-wheeler and commercial segments.

If there was one unofficial slogan to emerge from the auto shows, it was: get more cars, pay less. In fact, there has never been a better time to buy a car in Nepal, or switch from an older model to a new one. Even now, with a range of alternatives at each and every price point, customers can easily get overwhelmed by what exactly to pick.

Things have evolved since my column in this space a year ago, which reported that Nepal’s EV market was peaking. It is still peaking, but what is peaking now is a price war.

The headlines in China among its many EV manufacturers have now buffeted the Nepal market with aggressive pricing and offers for the customer base here.

Some examples of EVs that really disrupted the current market price mechanisms were: the Nammi Box, Nammi Vigo and the Deepal Nevo Q05. The hatch-back sized Nammi Box saw a Rs100,000 price reduction from its previous entry point of Rs3.099 million, whereas the Nammi Vigo compact SUV dropped to an eye-catching Rs3.799 million with the removal of some minor features such as a panoramic moonroof.

The Deepal Nevo Q05, on the other hand, might be marginally smaller than its bigger brother, the S05, but launched with an introductory offer of Rs4.699 million.

Soon enough, bigger players also announced price reductions and feature updates, such as BYD dropping the price of the highly sought after Atto 2 model from Rs4.899 million to Rs4.595 million, with the caveat that it has a smaller battery pack.

Similarly, the new Cherry QQ3, a crossover hatchback, launched at yet another aggressive introductory price of Rs3.099 million found itself undercutting another recently launched similar sized vehicle, the Proton Emas5, by just a couple of hundred rupees.

The mid-size SUV segment also saw price reductions such as with the Jaecoo J5 that was being offered at Rs4.799 million with a smaller battery configuration. The J5 was first launched at last year's NAIMA Expo at Rs6.099 million. Similarly, Leapmotor decreased the price of its recently launched B03X from Rs4.699 million to Rs4.499 million, keeping up the competition.

Larger premium vehicles EVs were not exempt from this wave. BYD launched an updated Sealion 7 with a bigger 150 kW motor (previously capped at 99 kW due to tax brackets) at Rs9.3 million and the Leapmotor C10 now sells for Rs7.599 million.

The price war meant that customers could quickly move up in segment size, features and range if they were willing to shell out a couple of extra lakhs as the hefty price tag between segments blurred.

But all this battle for the buyer also poses one great question: what about after-sales? The recent death of a driver in Bharatpur after his EV caught fire has put a spotlight on maintenance and safety.

EV’s, unlike traditional ICEs, cannot be serviced and maintained just anywhere. The cost of keeping and maintaining inventory of spare parts and of skilled workers is high. The question is, will importers keep their promise or falter down the line?

After the floods, deliveries to customers who booked their vehicles at the auto shows have faced delays because the vehicles have been rerouted through the longer Korala checkpoint in Mustang.

Chinese EVs parked in Jomsom after entering Nepal via Korala in Mustang. Photo: SUSHILBABU THAKALI

This border point remains relatively underdeveloped and its ability to absorb a sudden diversion of containers and commercial traffic is uncertain. Even so, nearly 700 Chinese EVs have entered Nepal through Korala since 26 August.

Even the EVs coming in from Korala and the vehicles imported from the Indian border are affected by the two-week landslide breach on the Prithvi Highway.

For importers, such uncertainties are likely to translate into longer transit times, more complicated logistics, and ultimately higher costs against the backdrop of price wars. How much of that burden will eventually hit consumers remains unclear.

With key trade routes still vulnerable to late-monsoon highway disruptions, the risks to both supply and pricing are becoming increasingly difficult to ignore.

publisher.title: Time Magazine
full_article: Such a transition would not be easy for Nepal. Its infrastructure, businesses and reputation are all geared toward cheap mass tourism. Bhutan’s high-value tourism model benefits from a rarity value: foreign tourists with the exception of Indians have never had easy access to the country. Costa Rica has protected more than a quarter of its landmass in national parks, creating thousands of square miles of protected wilderness for tourists to visit. Other established mass-market destinations, like Thailand, are attempting a similar transition. Nepal could do so, too, but the shift would reduce exposure to disasters only if high-end hotels were built out of harm’s way and the infrastructure supporting them were made resilient.

Key Takeaways:

USAC raised $30,406 through its Nepal Flood Relief Campaign

Donations came from executive committee members and Nepali community in the US

Association covered $40 transfer fee separately so full amount reached the fund

Campaign record, donor list and receipt made public for transparency

The United Sherpa Association of Colorado (USAC) has deposited $30,406 in the Prime Minister's Disaster Relief Fund for victims of the August 26 floods along the Bhotekoshi–Trishuli corridors.

Related Articles BYD, Cimex contribute Rs 70 million to PM's Disaster Relief Fund PM Balen Shah Reached Nuwakot by Road to Inspect Flood-Hit Bidur

The amount was raised through the association's Nepal Flood Relief Campaign, with contributions from its executive committee members and Nepali community members in the United States.

USAC President Lhakpa Sherpa said the campaign received strong support from the community and raised the full amount through collective donations. The association transferred the money to the relief fund on September 14, covering the $40 international transfer fee separately so that the entire donated amount could be deposited.

publisher.title: Variety
full_article:
Nepal‘s Academy Awards entry “Elephants in the Fog” is the sole Nepali film at the Toronto Film Festival, where director Abinash Bikram Shah has turned the film’s international visibility toward the floods devastating communities back home – among them people directly connected to the production.

Lead actress Puspa Thing Lama is from Nuwakot district, one of the worst-affected areas. Co-producer Prachanda Man Singh Shrestha, also from Nuwakot, has lost his home. “There is something difficult about watching a film travel internationally while people close to it are dealing with the loss of homes and livelihoods,” Shah tells Variety .

The production has already held a fundraising screening in Kathmandu, channeling the proceeds to the Prime Minister Disaster Relief Fund, and has worked with the Zonta Club and Rotary Clubs on support for children caught in the Bhotekoshi flooding. On Sept. 17, the film’s French production and distribution partners are staging a Paris screening, with Nepal’s Ambassador to France among those expected to attend; the evening’s distributor revenue will go to Nepal’s flood-relief fund. “We know that a film cannot solve a disaster,” Shah says. “But cinema can gather people in a room, create attention and sometimes turn that attention into action.”

The floods have also complicated the local release in Nepal. “It is hard to ask people to go to a cinema when many are dealing with displacement, loss and uncertainty,” he says. Despite that, “Elephants in the Fog” has carried into its second week since opening Sept. 4, taking in some NPR69 lakh ($45,000) in its first seven days. “But the conversations after screenings have meant just as much to us as the box office,” Shah says.

At the center of the film is Pirati, matriarch of a Kinnar community in a forested Nepalese village, played by first-time screen actress Puspa Thing Lama, who has spent decades as an LGBTIQA+ rights advocate. “She is not simply a representative of a ‘third gender’ community. She is a mother and a leader, with authority, affection, fears and contradictions,” Shah says.

Lama traveled to Cannes when the film took the Un Certain Regard Jury Prize and is now in Toronto. “There is something powerful about seeing someone who has spent decades working to make her community visible now occupying these spaces in her own right, not as a subject being discussed, but as an artist whose performance is being recognized,” Shah says. The Asia Pacific Screen Awards have nominated her for best performance; the film also picked up nods for best film and best director.

“I was drawn to the Kinnar community because of the richness and complexity of the community beyond the marginalization,” he says. The relationships between the women gradually became the film’s core – a story about mothers and daughters, and about people creating family when the structures around them have rejected them.

Sales company Best Friend Forever has closed deals across 14 territories. New agreements place the film with MetFilm Distribution in the U.K., Filmin in Spain, Vedette in Benelux, Trigon in Switzerland, Lev Cinema in Israel, Jayantii in Australia, EFAR Films in India, PT Falcon in Indonesia, the Film Development Council of the Philippines and Silk Route for inflight. Those join previously announced deals with Arizona Distribution and Les Valseurs Distribution in France, missingFILMs in Germany and Austria, Imovision in Brazil and The Tea Folks Films for domestic Nepal distribution. A pan-Latin America deal is expected shortly; North American rights are in advanced negotiations.

“The film has traveled much further than we ever expected, but its meaning remains rooted in the place where it began,” Shah says.
